1:
When the rest came is disputed. Ellicott says no intimation is given of how long after the removal of the ark this was, and holds that the narrative stands here not because it followed chronologically but because it is closely related in subject; it must have been after the successful close of the principal foreign wars, and more likely in a time of quiet prosperity than in his latter troubles. Clarke places it earlier, after the Philistines were cast out of the strong places they held in Israel but before he carried his arms beyond the land against the Moabites, Syrians and Idumeans. Henry draws from the fact that though David was a man of war he was for peace and did not delight in it, that he had not been long at rest nor would be long before he was at war again, and that he was in his element meditating in the law.

Nathan enters the history here, and the two who notice it differ on how much we know. Gill observes that who Nathan was and whence he came is not known, though he was plainly a man of great piety and prudence, familiar with David and perhaps dwelling in his palace; he reports a Jewish tradition identifying him with a nephew of David, which he thinks not very likely. Ellicott takes the first mention as no sign of obscurity, since Nathan was already a confidential counsellor, and he and Gad the seer wrote parts of the history of this reign and the next. On the curtains Clarke says simply the tabernacle, covered with the skins of beasts, where Ellicott notes that although the word is the one used in Exodus for the tabernacle covering, the ark was not now within that but in a similar temporary structure.

Whether Nathan did wrong in approving is the real question, and the answers form a gradient. Clarke is mildest: Nathan judged as a pious and prudent man and not as a prophet, the prophets not being always under a divine afflatus but only at select times. Ellicott says much the same, that Nathan naturally thought the pious purpose must be right but spoke by his own sense of right and not by divine direction. Henry allows a mistake and has God correct it: Nathan spoke not in God's name but as a wise and good man, and what he said agreed with the revealed will of God although the secret will was otherwise. It was Christ's prerogative always to speak the mind of God, other prophets speaking it only when the spirit of prophecy was upon them; where they mistook, as Samuel did once and Nathan here, God soon rectified it. Gill goes further and makes it a fault in both men: since the time and the person were not pointed out in the word of God, they should have consulted the Lord, and in this they erred and were tacitly reproved. Wesley is sharpest: Nathan hastily approved before consulting God, as both he and David ought to have done in a matter of so great moment, and therefore meets with a rebuke and is forced to acknowledge his error and recant it.

Henry supplies the frame the others omit. David's thought is a grateful return, since when providence has done much for us it should set us contriving what we may do for God, and a good use of leisure. He sets David's palace against another: how different were the thoughts of David sitting in his from Nebuchadnezzar's walking in his, the one full of how to glorify God and the other of the might of his own power. And gracious souls, he adds, cannot enjoy their own accommodations while the church is under a cloud. Delitzsch simply lays out the shape of what follows: the desire, the refusal and counter-promise, and the prayer of thanksgiving.
4:
The question is not a question, and three say so: Clarke that the interrogative has the force of thou shalt not, Delitzsch that it involves a negative reply and that Chronicles accordingly reads thou shalt not, Ellicott that the Greek and Syriac translate it so. On why the answer came that same night Gill and Henry agree, that neither man should continue long in his error and David in his zeal take a hasty step; Henry adds why it came by Nathan rather than to David directly, since one prophet countermanding another would have left Nathan despised and David perplexed, and God chose to support the honour of his prophets.

Why David was refused divides them, and the division is methodological. Ellicott points out that no reason is given here, that calling David my servant shows the prohibition carried no divine displeasure, and that the only reason assigned anywhere is the one David gives later, that he had shed much blood and been a man of war. Those wars had been necessary and were never disapproved, yet the mere fact of blood unfitted him for the office. He then rejects the two reasons nearly all commentators find in the message itself, that God must first build David a house before David could build God one, and that the kingdom was not yet settled: neither is assigned in the divine word, and it is better to keep to what is assigned, however fitting the others seem. Delitzsch offers precisely the first, calling it not a mere play upon words but the deep general truth that God must first build a man's house before the man can build God's, and the second too, that while the land was disputed God's dwelling could take no form but a wanderer's tent. Henry supplies a third reason, a division of labour: David is a man of war who must enlarge the borders, and a sweet psalmist who must prepare psalms and settle the courses of the Levites, while his son's genius will better suit the building.

Henry makes most of the tent. God regards not outward pomp, and his presence was as surely with his people when the ark was in a tent; he did not dwell but walk, and yet was not weary. David calls the tabernacle a temple in the psalms, because it answered the intention of one though made of curtains; wise men value not the show while they have the substance, and David may have had sweeter communion in a house of curtains than any successor in the house of cedar. From God's silence to the rulers he draws the rule that only instituted worship is acceptable, and that it is better to have a tent of God's appointing than a temple of one's own inventing. Delitzsch reads tent and dwelling as one thing, a tent which was the dwelling, and observes that since a tent is a traveller's dwelling God appeared as if himself travelling; Wesley instead distinguishes them, the one the curtains and hangings within, the other the frame of boards and its coverings.

Two smaller cruxes remain. Where the text says God spoke to none of the tribes, Clarke prefers the parallel's judges, since the two Hebrew words differ by a single stroke that would be mistaken if a little effaced. Ellicott grants the single letter but keeps tribes, the same use for the judges sprung from them occurring elsewhere. On the place promised to Israel, Clarke and Ellicott agree there is no change of tense in the original and it should read have appointed and have planted, where Wesley and Delitzsch keep the future. Gill and Wesley converge on the punctuation, both holding that the parenthesis about Israel should close before the clause about rest, which concerns David alone; Wesley alone enters a condition, that the promise to Israel holds except they notoriously forsake God.
12:
Ellicott begins with the date. Many take the future tense about the seed that shall proceed from David as proof that Solomon was not yet born, which would fix the point in the reign; but the same expression might have been used after his birth, the future being an assimilation to the futures running through the passage. How much of the promise is Solomon's and how much the Messiah's governs the rest, and two set out a rule for it. Wesley divides the passage by parts, some of David's posterity in general, some of Solomon, some of Christ only, and applies the rule strictly: where Solomon was a type the sense passes through him to Christ, but the clause about committing iniquity cannot touch Christ, who never committed any, so that branch is terminated in Solomon. Ellicott's rule is not division but succession: the promise plainly has a human successor in view, yet the establishment for ever, repeated three times, can only be fulfilled in the Messiah, and the explanation is the same as with the prophet promised through Moses, a long line of men filling the place of the true Prophet and King, all culminating in him.

The others apply one rule or the other without stating it. Delitzsch says it is very obvious from all the details that the promise related primarily to Solomon. Clarke takes the throne established for ever as the government of the spiritual kingdom, illustrated from the prophet's words about the increase of his government and peace. Gill keeps both in view, Solomon building the house and his antitype the Messiah another, and Solomon a son by adopting grace where Christ is Son by natural and eternal generation.

The rod of men produces a flat contradiction. Delitzsch rejects the reading that makes it moderate punishment such as parents inflict, insisting it means the punishments inflicted on all men who go astray, from which even the seed of David is not excepted. Henry and Wesley take exactly the reading he rejects. Wesley glosses it as rods that are gentle and moderate and suited to man's weakness; Henry offers two senses and prefers the softer, either a rod such as men may wield, so that God will not plead against him with his great power, or rather one such as men may bear, God considering his frame and correcting with all tenderness, not a stroke or a wound but a gentle touch. Clarke adds a warning of another kind, that many have used these verses to support unconditional final perseverance, that the text has nothing to do with it, and that pressing it would ruin the doctrine, since there is neither proof nor evidence of Solomon's salvation.

On the mercy that shall not depart Gill says it is not special grace but the kind that can be taken away, as it was from Saul; Wesley makes it plainly the kingdom; Clarke draws the contrast to its end, that Saul's family became totally extinct while David's remained until the incarnation, Joseph and Mary being both of it, so that Jesus was the only heir, who did not choose the secular throne but ascended the spiritual one. Ellicott notices that two different Hebrew words stand behind the one word established, the second better rendered made sure, refuses the Greek alteration of before thee into before me, and reads the verse as the last narrowing of an old promise: given first to the human race, then to the nation descended from Abraham, then to the tribe of Judah, and now to the family of David. On the word vision the two part again, Delitzsch insisting it was had waking and at night and not in a dream, the term being constantly distinguished from the word for dreaming, while Ellicott holds it applies to any divine communication and not merely to vision strictly so called.
18:
Whether David sat is disputed. Delitzsch denies it: the verb means remained or tarried, and the custom of sitting before the Lord in prayer cannot be deduced from the passage usually cited, where Moses is made to sit by exhaustion. Henry reports the Jewish claim that the kings of David's house alone might sit in the temple, refuses to let that justify the gesture in ordinary prayer, and offers two escapes: David took his place before the Lord, or continued there, meditating in silence and standing up to pray as the manner was. Wesley takes the same way out, sitting for a season while meditating and then altering his posture. Ellicott lets the sitting stand, as meditation before thanksgiving, praise and prayer. Clarke supplies an eastern parallel, that a suppliant seeking a favour seats himself in silence before a superior, or before the idol in a waiting posture.

The hardest clause is the one our version turns into a question about the manner of men, and it gets four answers. Ellicott says the Hebrew is obscure and the versions give little help, that the word rendered manner never bears that sense elsewhere, its established meaning being law, and that no question is intended at all: read it as an exclamation, and this is a law for man, David marvelling that so great a promise should come to such as himself. Clarke renders it more literally as the law of Adam, and asks whether David reaches back to the promise that the seed of the woman should bruise the serpent's head, so that from his line the Messiah should spring. Henry keeps the question and doubles it, asking whether man can expect such dealing from his Maker and whether men deal thus with one another; but he also passes on the other reading and draws a doctrine from it, that one whose kingdom is established for ever must be a man and yet the Lord Jehovah, so a Messiah from David's loins must be man, but reigning for ever must be God. Wesley keeps the question and answers it: men do not use their inferiors so, and this is the prerogative of divine grace.

The plural verb in the verse on the redemption of Israel divides Henry from Ellicott completely. Henry hears the Trinity in it, the same consultation of all the persons about redemption as about creation, when God said, Let us make man. Ellicott explains it otherwise: the plural name always takes a singular verb when it means the true God, and the verb is plural here because the thought is, what nation is there whom its gods went to redeem? He works two further difficulties in the verse: the words for you can only mean Israel and sit strangely in a prayer to God, being dropped by the Greek and altered to for them by the Latin, so if kept they mark David turning a moment to the people; and for thy land stands where the Greek and the parallel have by driving out, which would remove the need to supply a word the Hebrew lacks.

Two smaller notes remain. On what David heard with his ears Ellicott holds it unnecessary to confine the phrase to oral tradition, since the same word is used of written records elsewhere, so David means the history of God's dealings recorded in their sacred books. Henry reads for thy word's sake either of Christ the eternal Word, all being owing to his merit, or of God magnifying his word of promise above all his name; Wesley keeps it to faithfulness, that God might fulfil what he promised, and takes according to thine own heart as mere liberality without desert, remarking how far David was, gracious man as he was, from thinking his actions meritorious. Gill adds that David went into the tabernacle he had prepared for the ark.
25:
Clarke turns the last section into an argument, the longest thing in the chapter. He begins by insisting the promises were conditional: David's posterity did not walk with God and were driven from the throne, so the promises have failed to his natural posterity and are fulfilled to Christ and his spiritual seed alone. He then takes up a deistical writer who argued that no promise of a Messiah can be recorded here, and answers three objections. To the first, that the prosperity described was never the fate of the Jews, he replies that the verbs should be past or present, so the sense is that God has appointed a place for Israel and has planted them, a rendering our translators allow elsewhere in the passage. To the second, that the son who builds a house must be Solomon, he replies that the house God promised was not material but a spiritual family, to be raised up after David slept with his fathers, words which exclude Solomon, who was set on the throne before David died. To the third, that the Messiah could not commit iniquity, he answers by grammar, that the Hebrew verb is passive, so the clause reads even in his suffering for iniquity, with the rod due to men and the stripes due to the children of Adam.

From this he draws a conclusion the others will not. If the Messiah is meant here, suffering innocently for the sins of others, then Solomon cannot be, and the prophecy cannot admit a double sense or be applied to two such opposite characters. He puts the Ethiopian's question to it, of whom speaketh the prophet this, and answers that it can only be one. That is a flat refusal of the way Wesley, Ellicott and Delitzsch read the promise, by division, by succession, or as relating primarily to Solomon. Clarke also reads David's exclusion outward into a general rule, that God seldom employs a soldier in spiritual work for the same reason given to David, and illustrates it from a dragoon turned preacher who reformed many hundreds in the army and was persuaded that in all his battles he had never killed a man, though he would have slain the whole opposing army had it been in his power.

The shape of the prayer is agreed. Delitzsch divides it into thanksgiving for the promise and supplication for its fulfilment, summed up again in the two clauses beginning with and now. Henry notices that David returned his answer to God himself and did not send it by Nathan, since when ministers deliver God's message it is not to them but to God that our hearts must reply; and he grounds the petitions on the message, David asking only what God has already revealed. Gill passes on the Targum's rendering of the last request as begin and bless, so the promised blessings might begin to descend and give some encouragement that the whole would be fulfilled.

Two last readings. Ellicott suggests the closing words may be a future rather than a wish, a prophecy built on the promise rather than a petition, and compares a like ambiguity in the last clause of an old hymn; he adds that although several psalms have been referred to this point in David's life, none carries a note of time fixing it here, unless the one that reads like an inspired interpretation of the promise of perpetuity. On the petition that God's name be magnified he observes that David puts the hallowing of the name first, in the true spirit of the Lord's Prayer, and that this was the striking feature of his whole life, whatever sins he was at times betrayed into. Gill makes the same petition turn on the Messiah, and Wesley reduces it to the plainest sense, that God should never cease to manifest himself as the God and governor of Israel.
